content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2015. Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is a neuromodulatory therapy used as an adjunctive treatment for individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy. VNS involves the delivery of chronic, intermittent electrical stimulation to the vagus nerve via a programmable pulse generator. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of VNS as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted on March 3, 2022, using the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS) and MEDLINE Ovid, without language restrictions. The CRS Web includes randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from various sources, including Cochrane Review Groups, CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The review included randomized, double-blind, controlled trials of VNS as an add-on therapy. These trials compared highand low-level stimulation (using rapid, mild, and slow duty-cycle paradigms), VNS stimulation versus no stimulation, or VNS versus another intervention. Participants included adults and children with drug-resistant focal seizures who were either ineligible for surgery or had previously failed surgical treatment. The review followed standard Cochrane methods and assessed the following outcomes: (1) a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, (2) treatment withdrawal for any reason, (3) adverse effects, (4) quality of life (QoL), (5) cognition, and (6) mood. No new studies were identified for this update, so the conclusions remain unchanged. The review included five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from the previous update, involving a total of 439 participants. The baseline phase of these studies ranged from 4 to 12 weeks, and the double-blind treatment phases lasted between 12 and 20 weeks. Two studies were rated as having a low risk of bias, while three were rated as having an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting of study design details. Effective blinding in VNS studies is challenging because stimulation-related side effects, such as voice alteration, are common. The risk ratio (RR) for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency was 1.73 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.13 to 2.64; 4 RCTs, 373 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), indicating that high-frequency VNS was more than 1.5 times as effective as low-frequency VNS. The RR for treatment withdrawal was 2.56 (95% CI 0.51 to 12.71; 4 RCTs, 375 participants; low-certainty evidence). The most frequently reported adverse events were as follows: Hoarseness: RR 2.17 (99% CI 1.49 to 3.17; 3 RCTs, 330 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) Cough: RR 1.09 (99% CI 0.74 to 1.62; 3 RCTs, 334 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) Dyspnoea: RR 2.45 (99% CI 1.07 to 5.60; 3 RCTs, 312 participants; low-certainty evidence) Pain: RR 1.01 (99% CI 0.60 to 1.68; 2 RCTs, 312 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) Paraesthesia: RR 0.78 (99% CI 0.39 to 1.53; 2 RCTs, 312 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) Two studies (312 participants) reported a small number of favorable QoL effects associated with VNS stimulation, but the results were inconclusive when comparing highand low-level stimulation groups. One study (198 participants) found no conclusive differences between highand low-level stimulation in terms of cognitive outcomes across all measures used. Another study (114 participants) reported that most participants experienced mood improvement on the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale compared to baseline, but the results were inconclusive between highand low-level stimulation groups. No significant heterogeneity was observed between studies for any of the outcomes. In conclusion, VNS appears to be an effective and well-tolerated treatment for focal seizures. High-level stimulation was shown to reduce seizure frequency more effectively than low-level stimulation. The low rate of treatment withdrawals suggests that VNS is generally well tolerated. Adverse effects associated with VNS implantation and stimulation included hoarseness, cough, dyspnoea, pain, paraesthesia, nausea, and headache. Hoarseness and dyspnoea were more likely to occur with high-level stimulation than low-level stimulation. However, the evidence for these outcomes is of moderate to low certainty. Further high-quality research is needed to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of VNS for drug-resistant focal seizures.
